ami_style_notes: The meeting has a casual, collegial video-call style with mostly short-to-medium conversational turns before and after much longer, highly structured presentation turns. Early small talk is loose and overlap-prone, with frequent greetings, quick acknowledgments (“yeah,” “okay,” “great”), repetitions, self-corrections, and occasional audio/logistics interruptions. Speakers hedge often with “um,” “I think,” “sort of,” “maybe,” “I guess,” and “you know,” especially when speculating or answering questions. Formality is moderate: introductions and talk transitions are ceremonious, but the surrounding interaction is friendly, joking, and informal. Participants generally challenge ideas indirectly, framing concerns as “a question,” “I’m curious,” or “have you looked at…,” and presenters respond affirmingly before qualifying limits or uncertainty. Questions are usually prefaced by praise or disclaimers (“great talk,” “naive question,” “quick question”), then develop into multi-part, exploratory prompts. Technical speakers use repeated signposting, rhetorical questions, restatements, and simple verbal transitions to guide listeners through complex material.
research_problem: Understanding how urban green space affects mental health outcomes in low-income communities

speakers.name: Dr. Maya Okafor
speakers.background: Dr. Okafor is a postdoctoral landscape ecologist with four years of post-PhD research on urban habitat networks, following six years of graduate fieldwork in Midwestern and East Coast cities. She combines GIS-based land-cover mapping, street-level vegetation audits, bird and pollinator surveys, and patch-network models to study how parks, tree corridors, gardens, and restored vacant lots function as urban ecological systems.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Maya treats green space as a spatially structured habitat network rather than a simple count of nearby parks. She wants the site-selection framework to distinguish area, vegetation quality, maintenance, and connectivity among green patches, while remaining cautious about how ecological indicators can be validly linked to residents' mental-health outcomes.
speakers.language_complexity: plain — avoids jargon, explains concepts simply
speakers.epistemic_stance: uncertain about how their methods apply to this problem

speakers.name: Dr. Luis Herrera
speakers.background: Dr. Herrera is a medical anthropologist with 14 years of community-based research experience in disinvested urban neighborhoods. His work uses participant observation, walking interviews, oral histories, neighborhood ethnography, and collaborative interview design to examine how housing insecurity, policing, caregiving, and public-space use shape everyday stress and well-being.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Luis is concerned that formal measures of green-space access may mistake visibility or mapped proximity for usable, safe, socially meaningful space. He will press the team to learn how residents define a park, whether they feel able to use it, who controls it, and how histories of neglect or redevelopment affect what greening means locally. He is skeptical of protocols that treat neighborhood exposure as interchangeable across communities.
speakers.language_complexity: moderate — balances jargon with accessible language

speakers.name: Dr. Priya Nanduri
speakers.background: Dr. Nanduri is a cognitive-affective neuroscience postdoctoral researcher with five years of experience studying stress, attention, and mood using resting-state fMRI, EEG, salivary cortisol, and validated symptom scales. Her recent work examines whether repeated environmental exposures are associated with changes in neural systems involved in emotion regulation and threat monitoring.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Priya sees mental-health effects as potentially operating through stress physiology and brain systems supporting attention, affect regulation, and rumination. She wants measures that can relate residents' reported contact with green environments to symptom assessments and feasible neural or physiological data, while deferring to community and ecological experts about what counts as meaningful neighborhood exposure.
speakers.language_complexity: moderate — balances jargon with accessible language
speakers.epistemic_stance: defers to other experts outside their domain

benchmark_task: Give a meeting transcript where two researchers from different disciplines use the same term with different discipline-specific definitions. The evaluated AI must identify both meanings and associate each with the correct discipline.

seed_spec.benchmark_task: Give a meeting transcript where two researchers from different disciplines use the same term with different discipline-specific definitions. The evaluated AI must identify both meanings and associate each with the correct discipline.
seed_spec.explicit_instruction: Create a planning-meeting transcript involving at least an ecologist and a neuroscientist, with an anthropologist participating in ordinary study-design discussion. The ecologist and neuroscientist must each use the word "connectivity" naturally and unambiguously in their own discipline-specific sense, without initially noticing that they mean different things. The ecologist knows connectivity as the degree to which green-space patches are physically linked or traversable for organisms; the neuroscientist knows connectivity as functional coupling or coordinated activity between brain regions measured from neural data. Keep the difference implicit rather than having participants explain or resolve it. Include concrete discussion of the proposed urban-green-space and mental-health study, but do not introduce any additional conflicting uses of technical terms that could obscure the target. No participant should state the benchmark task or provide a meta-analysis of the ambiguity.

meanings.meaning: The physical or ecological linkage among green-space patches that allows organisms, propagules, or ecological processes to move between them.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Okafor
transcript.text: Hi, everyone. Thanks for making time—can you all hear me okay? Great. I was hoping today we could get clear on what we need to observe before we choose sites, because I don't think park acreage or nearest-park distance will capture the, the ecological differences among these neighborhoods.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Luis Herrera
transcript.text: Yeah, exactly. I’d want us to separate what’s present from what people can actually use day to day. On the preliminary walks by the garden cluster, caregivers kept calling the garden “for the school,” while the little shaded step- the shaded stoop across the street was where people said they actually stopped and talked. So an amenities inventory would get that backwards.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Priya Nanduri
transcript.text: Mm, that's really important.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Okafor
transcript.text: Yes, and that is exactly why I would not want a single access measure. Luis, when residents say they “have a park,” are they usually naming the closest mapped park, or the place they actually use? For the ecological side, those can be very different networks—especially where a road, fence, or poor maintenance breaks what looks connected on the map.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Luis Herrera
transcript.text: Usually, they name the place they can actually fit into a day, where a child can be watched and somebody they know is sitting, not necessarily the nearest park. I think we should ask that separately. What places count as green space to you, and where have you actually spent time this week? The gap between those answers may be what we need to explain.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Priya Nanduri
transcript.text: And for us, that gap may matter more than a generic exposure score. We could ask about usual routes and routine outdoor stops, not just visits, and pair that with brief repeated stress and affect ratings, because in our pilot, the more consistent signal was people whose outdoor time was built into daily, daily life. Luis, does a route-based prompt feel workable in interviews?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Luis Herrera
transcript.text: It can work if we let people start with a typical day instead of handing them a route to account for. A caregiver might say, you know, "I walk to school, then I wait on that stoop," and that gives us the route, plus who they're with and whether it feels available. But I'd want an option to do it seated, with a map or just a narrative, because walking interviews won't be comfortable or feasible for everybody, especially if...—

transcript.speaker: Dr. Priya Nanduri
transcript.text: Right, that makes sense.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Okafor
transcript.text: That would also let us map the actual pedestrian network instead of assuming a straight-line buffer around each site. If people describe a route, we can note the road crossings, fenced edges, shade, and the small planted patches along it. Those may be the features that make a tree corridor function, or not function, as a connected green route. I’m a little cautious, though, about calling that ecological connectivity without field checks.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Luis Herrera
transcript.text: The field check has to include who can linger there, not just whether the planting is continuous. A route may be technically walkable, but then- but it may cross a block where people feel watched or unwelcome. I can build prompts around those breaks and ask local partners what observation on the housing-complex blocks would feel acceptable.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Okafor
transcript.text: For the site audit, I can keep two linked records. One is the physical permeability of the green network, so canopy gaps, crossings, fences, vegetation condition. And the other is the resident-reported social breaks along the same route. I wouldn't fold those into one connectivity score, but comparing them may show us where the aerial layer is, is misleading us, like on the east-side corridor.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Luis Herrera
transcript.text: That split sounds right. I'd also want the social breaks to be resident-defined before we, we code them too tightly. Sometimes it's not a fixed feature, but a time of day or who happens to be on the block. I can test that in the interviews. Where along a usual route do you change your behavior, and what makes that place different?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Priya Nanduri
transcript.text: That time-of-day piece is useful for us too, because a place can be physically connected but not provide a reliable restorative exposure if people only move through it under stress. When I say connectivity, I mean neural connectivity, obviously, but it makes me wonder whether any small physiological subset should capture repeated routine contact across days rather than a single visit—we'd otherwise be measuring current state more than the pattern of exposure.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Okafor
transcript.text: That seems sensible. For a subset, I could characterize routine-contact routes at two or three points over the study period, rather than treating the baseline audit as fixed. Pruning, lot maintenance, and garden access can change quickly. I just wouldn't infer that a corridor's ecological function is the mechanism for a stress result without keeping those measures separate.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Priya Nanduri
transcript.text: That gives us a more defensible time-varying exposure measure. I’d like the brief symptom and momentary-stress sampling to line up with those route windows, maybe a few days at each wave, so we can separate a bad day from- so we can tell whether someone’s usual outdoor contact has actually changed. The neural piece, if we do it at all, probably belongs after we see whether that repeated field protocol is tolerable.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Okafor
transcript.text: I can support that with repeat audits, but we should check what the city records can actually tell us. The land-cover layer may miss a lot that changes between waves, especially recently greened lots and maintenance work, so I'll check whether current parcel and maintenance records are available before we build the exposure measure around...

transcript.speaker: Dr. Luis Herrera
transcript.text: Before those records start driving site selection, I should check them against what local partners say has actually changed in use or, I mean, in meaning. A lot that was recently greened can read as neighborhood care to one group and as a redevelopment signal to another, and that changes whether people will spend time there at all.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Okafor
transcript.text: I can treat those records as a change-detection lead rather than ground truth. We can flag parcels with recent work, then verify the vegetation condition, access, and maintenance in the field. For site selection, I think we need a mix that deliberately separates a large park, the garden-and-lot clusters, and the apparent tree corridor, even if their mapped green-area totals overlap.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Priya Nanduri
transcript.text: That mix would let us test whether routine contact, not just total greenness, is what tracks stress and mood. On the assessment side, I'd keep the core protocol light, with baseline symptom measures and then a few days of brief momentary ratings at each audit wave. Then we can use the site types to make sure we're not really just comparing park proximity, and...

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Okafor
transcript.text: Mm, okay.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Luis Herrera
transcript.text: Mm, and for those waves, can we avoid making participation depend on people being visibly out in the neighborhood at particular times? Some folks, especially around the complexes, may have caregiving constraints or may not want to be seen doing a study walk. I can check with partners whether seated route narratives and phone, phone check-ins would feel acceptable alongside the momentary ratings.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Priya Nanduri
transcript.text: The momentary ratings can be phone-based and completed wherever someone is, so we should be clear that they’re sampling current stress and context, not checking that anyone went outside. We can ask whether they’ve had routine outdoor contact since the last prompt without requiring a location trace, and then the seated route narrative gives us that richer exposure context.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Luis Herrera
transcript.text: That feels much safer. I’d add one open-ended check-in at each wave, something like, “was there a place outside that mattered to your day, or that you avoided?” A yes/no contact item can miss the stoop, the bus-stop tree, or a change in who feels welcome. I’ll talk with the partners this week about the complexes and what recruitment language won’t make people feel monitored.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Okafor
transcript.text: And that open-ended item may also catch small sites that never show up in a park-access measure. I’ll make sure our audit form can link any places residents name to the nearest patch or route segment, without assuming that named place is the ecological unit we score. Then we can see what’s, what’s being missed on the ground.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Priya Nanduri
transcript.text: That gives us a way to preserve what contact means without turning it into passive tracking. I can fold that open-ended check-in into the phone protocol and code it alongside the brief affect and stress ratings. We may find that a named place matters even on days when someone reports very, very little time outdoors. For this first round, I think that’s more valuable than stretching for EEG.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Luis Herrera
transcript.text: Yeah, that’s promising.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Okafor
transcript.text: I agree, it's better to keep the first round focused on repeatable field and route measures, and then...

transcript.speaker: Dr. Luis Herrera
transcript.text: Okay, I think we should leave it there. I’ll follow up by email once I’ve spoken with the partners this week. Thanks, thanks everybody.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Okafor
transcript.text: Thank you, Luis. Take care, everyone.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Priya Nanduri
transcript.text: Thanks, both—bye.
